items.title: The gun within: Crimes involving police officers rise to 248
items.description: Report reveals an increase in cases of officers pointing guns at their colleagues and themselves.
content: Crime incidents also include suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
Police constable Raphael Ojiambo, 24, was shot dead at the Wikithuki Border Patrol Unit training camp in Tseikuru, Kitui County on October 25, 2024.
Investigations pointed to the young officer being killed by another constable, Hussein Yusuf Ali, who was arrested three kilometres from the camp a day later.
The two officers had recently graduated from the Administration Police Training College in Embakasi and were undergoing further training before deployment to the Border Patrol Unit.

In Eldoret, Uasin Gishu County, police constable Lillian Biwott was arrested on September 5, 2026, after allegedly shooting and killing her husband, Victor Kipchumba, following a long-running family dispute.
Biwott, an Administration Police officer attached to the Kenya Bureau of Standards, reportedly returned home after reporting for duty before the argument escalated into the shooting.
Crime incidents also include suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
Uasin Gishu County Police Commander Benjamin Mwanthi confirmed that the suspect was being held and would be arraigned in court.
The two are among more than 250 crime incidents involving police officers in the past year.
A report on national security tabled before Parliament by President William Ruto has revealed that crimes involving police officers increased to 248 between September, 2025 and August, 2026.
Since conclusion of the report, there have been more incidents, for instance the murder of Raphael Ojiambo.

The National Police Service has advertised for recruitment of officers, less than a year after a similar exercise that netted 10,000 new recruits. A source at the NPS said that the fresh exercise is targeting 5,000 recruits.

As part of initiatives to lower the number of crimes involving police officers, the National Police Service Commission has established a counselling unit to support officers facing mental-health and substance-abuse challenges. Police authorities have also acknowledged the trauma associated with maintaining law and order in difficult circumstances.

On January 14, 2026, a Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) ranger, John Ndichu, allegedly shot dead Police Constable Stanley Karithi in Kinango, Kwale County, following a disagreement over two goats reportedly collected for Christmas festivities.
The ranger also shot and wounded another police officer and a boda boda rider before turning his weapon on himself.

In some cases, the violence has unfolded inside police stations and officers’ quarters. In others, it has spilled into homes, workplaces and public spaces, leaving families devastated and raising concerns about the safeguards governing the use of government-issued weapons.

According to police accounts, the disagreement arose after officers questioned Ndichu about two goats allegedly donated by a rancher for Christmas celebrations but which had not been handed over as expected.
The ranger reportedly became angry, picked up his AK-47 rifle and opened fire.
The incident illustrated how seemingly minor disputes between personnel serving in uniformed agencies can escalate into deadly confrontations when firearms are readily accessible.
Away from the workplace, a series of incidents involving serving officers has also raised concerns about domestic violence and the use of service weapons in family disputes.

On July 20, 2026, Administration Police Sergeant John Kamau Ikenye allegedly shot dead his partner, Betha Wanja Gachoki, before turning his G3 rifle on himself at their staff quarters at Karoti Girls High School in Mwea East, Kirinyaga County.
The bodies were discovered after colleagues became concerned when Ikenye failed to report for duty.
Preliminary investigations indicated that Wanja had sustained gunshot wounds while lying in bed, while the officer was found seated in the sitting room with the rifle.
A neighbour, who said the couple had lived together for about three years, expressed disbelief at the tragedy.

“I used to buy items from his wife’s shop. They were very friendly. The lady comes from Difathas and they had been together for three years. We wonder what went wrong,” said Kimbimbi resident Stella Wangui.

Another neighbour said residents had heard gunshots but did not immediately appreciate their significance.

“We heard gunshots at around 4am but did not take them seriously. Later, we were shocked to learn that a police officer had killed his wife and then committed suicide. We suspect they may have quarrelled, although we do not know the cause,” the neighbour said.

The incident followed another shooting in Naivasha on January 1, 2026, when Corporal Collins Kochei allegedly shot Lucy Wanjiru Njoroge, a 34-year-old bar owner, before turning his AK-47 rifle on himself.
Kochei, who was attached to Tangi Tano Police Post in Gilgil, died after being rushed to hospital, while Njoroge was admitted in critical condition.
Detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations launched investigations into the shooting.
The incidents have also included suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
On February 17, 2026, Constable Joseph Komolomoi was found dead in his house at Forolle Police Lines in Marsabit County after allegedly shooting himself with his AK-47 rifle.
Colleagues reportedly heard a gunshot before breaking into the locked house and finding his body.
A note was recovered from the house, although police said it would undergo forensic examination to establish its authenticity.
On May 14, 2026, a police constable attached to Daystar Police Post in Athi River reportedly shot himself at his residence following a domestic disagreement with his 23-year-old spouse.
He was rushed to hospital in Mlolongo before being transferred to another facility in Kikuyu, where he later died.
A police report indicated that the firearm used had been officially issued to him. Investigators recovered a Scorpion rifle and a spent 9mm cartridge from the scene.
On June 2, 2026, another officer attached to the Diplomatic Police Unit and assigned to a Member of Parliament was found dead in his rented house in Kasarani, Nairobi.
Police recovered his service firearm and treated the incident as a suspected suicide pending investigations.

In Laikipia, Constable Peter Macharia Mwangi shot and killed 29-year-old Benson Kipkemboi Chirchir on December 14, 2025, before returning to his patrol base in Ndurumo, Rumuruti, and shooting himself.

Another officer attached to Ahero Police Station in Kisumu was found hanging in his house on January 21, 2026. According to an incident report, the officer had previously complained to colleagues about stress linked to unresolved domestic issues.

Beyond the individual tragedies, the incidents raise questions about whether the police service has adequate systems to identify officers experiencing psychological distress, domestic problems or conflicts with colleagues before situations escalate.
They also raise questions about firearm management, particularly when an officer is facing a domestic challenges, disciplinary difficulties or other circumstances that affect mental health.

Gachagua accuses IEBC of state capture ahead of 2027 polls
items.description: DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua declared on Citizen TV's JKLive that no one will steal Kenya's 2027 General Election, accusing the IEBC of operating under state capture.
content: The impeached former Deputy President fires his sharpest warning yet — at the IEBC, President Ruto, and anyone who thinks they can steal the vote

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua returned to prime-time national television on Wednesday night with his most combative performance yet, declaring on Citizen TV’s JKLive that no one would steal the 10 August 2027 General Election on his watch — and accusing the country’s electoral commission of operating under state capture at the direction of President William Ruto.

The interview, broadcast to millions of Kenyans still weighing the country’s fractured political landscape, was not merely a television appearance. It was, in effect, the formal opening salvo of the most consequential election campaign Kenya has seen since 2002. Speaking in his capacity as leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, Gachagua was blunt: no one would be able to rig the election if he was involved, and he would be watching every step of the process.

“I’m an expert in elections; I’ve never lost a presidential election. I have supported presidential candidates even when it looked like it was not fashionable to support Ruto. The day I agreed to support him, he won,” he said, drawing an unmistakable line under his claim to be the opposition’s most formidable electoral strategist.

Kenya’s road to August 2027 is already deeply contested. At its centre stands Gachagua — impeached, unbowed, and operating with the energy of a man who believes history dealt him an injustice he intends to correct at the ballot box. His audience understands the subtext. The Mt Kenya region, which he commands as Kenya’s most populous and historically decisive voting bloc, is watching every move.

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission did not escape the night unscathed. Gachagua accused the IEBC chairman Erastus Ethekon of operating under government influence, alleging the electoral agency was being controlled by the Ministry of Interior. “The chairman is under state capture; IEBC is run by the Ministry of Interior,” he said during the JKLive interview. The IEBC has consistently denied any political interference and has stated publicly that it has nothing to hide.

The interview followed a dramatic day in which Gachagua, alongside United Green Movement leader David Maraga and Democratic Party leader Justin Muturi, boycotted a consultative meeting with the IEBC, claiming it had been organised not by the commission but by the State Department for Interior. “We are not willing to engage in a charade. The meeting this afternoon has been organised by the State Department of Interior. Why is William Ruto speaking for IEBC?” he said at a press briefing earlier in the day.

Gachagua announced that the United Opposition would mobilise Kenyans in January 2027 to engage the commission directly should concerns remain unaddressed. “William Ruto cannot threaten us. Next year in January, we will organise Kenyans to talk to IEBC directly,” he warned.

The accusations are serious — and structurally significant. Kenya’s elections have been disputed before, most catastrophically in 2007 and most controversially in 2017. The spectre of a 2027 contest in which the main opposition does not trust the umpire before a single ballot has been cast raises questions that go far beyond political theatre.

Gachagua has been building this case for weeks. Earlier this month, speaking at the opening of DCP’s Nairobi County offices in Kasarani, he accused the Registrar of Persons of deliberately delaying the issuance of national identity cards to young people in perceived opposition strongholds, claiming applicants in government-aligned areas received their IDs within two to three days while those in opposition areas waited up to seven months. The government dismissed the claims.

On Wednesday night he went further still, alleging that Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo had set aside KSh15 billion to finance political candidates targeting leaders allied to the late Raila Odinga in the 2027 election, with several senior government and parastatal officials expected to resign before 10 February 2027 to seek elective office under the alleged arrangement. Neither Omollo nor the government has responded to the specific allegations.

What gives Gachagua’s warnings their unusual weight is not merely his rhetoric — it is his record and his reach. Since his impeachment, he has constructed a political machine of remarkable speed and discipline. He has sought counsel from Kikuyu elders under the Kiama Kia Kiama leadership, whose guidance, he says, is shaping his strategy towards what he calls the formation of the “sixth administration.” He has opened party offices across the country, fielded candidates successfully in by-elections, and built what observers describe as the most organised opposition structure Kenya has seen heading into a general election.

In October, speaking on KTN, he predicted that the 2027 election would mirror Kenya’s 2002 moment — when opposition parties united behind Mwai Kibaki to end KANU’s decades-long grip on power. He warned that politicians who reject a joint opposition candidate risk political isolation. He has not publicly declared whether he will be that candidate — or whether he will play kingmaker instead — but the ambiguity appears deliberate.

On JKLive, Gachagua addressed the question of his eligibility directly, citing Article 99(3) of the Constitution to argue that he would qualify to be cleared as a presidential candidate. His lawyers have been pursuing the matter through the courts, and observers expect a ruling on his eligibility to become one of the defining legal battles of the pre-election period.

He has also prepared for the possibility of disqualification, revealing that he has identified a pool of young leaders capable of carrying the Mt Kenya region’s presidential bid if courts rule against him, dismissing suggestions that such a ruling would leave the region politically leaderless.

The political arithmetic of 2027 remains fluid. President Ruto retains the advantages of incumbency, state resources, and a party — the United Democratic Alliance — with deep organisational roots. But the economic pain of the past two years, the Gen Z uprising of 2024 that forced a cabinet reshuffle, and the continuing cost-of-living pressures have dented his approval ratings considerably. For many Kenyans, 2027 is not yet decided.

What Wednesday’s interview confirmed is that the campaign is now fully under way — raw, loud, and deeply personal. Gachagua is no longer simply a former official making allegations from the margins. He is the opposition’s most prominent voice, its most effective fundraiser, and arguably its most feared strategist. For a country with Kenya’s electoral history, the combination of a motivated opposition, a disputed umpire, and a sitting president fighting for his political survival makes August 2027 a date every Kenyan is already counting down to.

Whether the vote is clean, credible, and peaceful when it arrives will depend on choices made in the months between now and then. If Wednesday night’s interview is any guide, those months will not be quiet.

items.title: "Demand is huge": PSC explains how gov't will hire 50k interns in January 2027
items.description: Kenya’s PSC plans 50,000 government internships from January 2027, using a 10% staffing formula as 41,000 graduates compete for 8,000 places amid high demand.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Kenyan graduates could soon have far greater access to government internships after the Public Service Commission outlined plans to grow available placements from 8,000 to 50,000 starting January 2027, following a directive from President William Ruto during the 2026 Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret.

PSC Chairperson Francis Meja explained that the commission had settled on a standardised formula to bring predictability to how positions are spread across ministries, state departments, agencies and parastatals.
Each institution will be required to ring-fence internship slots equal to 10% of its approved staffing establishment, meaning an organisation with 1,000 approved posts would absorb 100 interns.

Previously, the National Treasury channelled roughly KSh 2 billion annually to fund approximately 8,000 internship positions. That figure, however, has long fallen short of demand. When the PSC last advertised 8,000 positions, it received 41,000 applications.
Meja described the internship scheme as a bridge between academic training and the job market, stressing that the target of 50,000 is a starting point rather than a ceiling.
German firm signs deal with Kenya to remove barriers for Kenyans seeking jobs abroad

Graduates who complete the programme will reportedly be given priority consideration when institutions post formal vacancies, although completing an internship does not guarantee permanent employment.

The PSC chairperson also revealed that talks with private-sector employers are progressing and that a further 50,000 positions are intended to be unlocked through industry partnerships by January 2027.

The PSC has opened applications for the 2026/2027 financial year, with the deadline set for December 14, 2026. Graduates are urged to apply only through the Commission's official recruitment platforms to avoid falling victim to fraudsters.

Elsewhere, TUKO also highlighted facts about the Public Service Commission’s 6,000 internship positions under the Affordable Housing Programme, including the fields on offer, eligibility requirements and application deadline.

The 12-month placements span technical and professional roles across the country, with 500 construction management slots among the largest allocations. Applications close on November 9, 2026, and candidates must have graduated from 2020 onwards.

"Move as fast": Payaza buys small businesses' platform to compete in Kenya
items.description: Payaza has acquired Ghana’s Seesail through Shopaza, adding SME commerce tools and talent as the payments firm expands into Kenya and across African markets.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Payaza Africa has acquired Seesail Technologies Ltd, a Ghana-founded commerce platform serving small businesses, through its Shopaza product days after the Lagos-based payments company formally entered Kenya.
Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The full Seesail team moves across to Shopaza, and Seesail co-founder and CEO Victor Blavo takes up the role of General Manager, Africa.

The acquisition did not come out of the blue. Seesail's merchants had already been processing payments through Payaza's infrastructure, giving Payaza's leadership an early vantage point on the team's performance before any ownership conversation began.

PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Payaza CEO Seyi Ebenezer described the deal as a conviction bet on a team that had achieved real traction with limited resources.
Payaza said every Seesail function joins Shopaza with its own budget from day one and the operational freedom to run independently, under guidance from the CEO.
The combined entity is designed to extend Shopaza's commerce infrastructure into access to finance and broader distribution for small and medium-sized enterprises across Africa.

Blavo built Seesail around a conviction shaped by his own family's experience. After his mother attempted to revive a restaurant business she had operated in Yaba, Lagos, following the family's relocation to Ghana, she found that affordable tools and financing were simply unavailable.
Kenya hosts government-endorsed Africa's Next Supermodel, winner claims KSh 645k
That gap became the founding premise of Seesail.
Before bootstrapping Seesail, Blavo accumulated experience across Nigerian, Ghanaian and international firms, including Chipper Cash.

As reported earlier on TUKO.co.ke, Payaza received authorisation from the Central Bank of Kenya on November 17, 2026, to operate as a payment service provider, landing in one of the continent's most active digital payments markets.
Founded in Lagos in 2022, the company now operates across 31 countries spanning Africa, North America, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates and Oceania.
Kenya's payments landscape offers significant scale. Mobile money transactions reached KSh 8.7 trillion in 2024, a figure equivalent to more than half of national GDP.
Payaza's local focus centres on cross-border transfer solutions, merchant acquiring infrastructure and e-commerce tools for merchants and exporters.
The Seesail acquisition broadens the SME toolkit Payaza can deploy across Kenya, Ghana and other markets as it competes with regional players including Paystack, Cellulant and Moniepoint.

Australia to Block Kenyans, Other Visitors From Shifting to Work, Student Visas in New Law
items.description: Australia will make condition 8503 mandatory on visitor visas from 28 November 2026, ending visa-hopping for Kenyans as stricter Bridging Visa B checks begin.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)
Australia is set to close a widely used migration loophole that allowed foreign visitors, including Kenyans, to switch to student, work, or other substantive visas without leaving the country.

Under the Migration Amendment (Preventing Further Stay for Visitor Visas) Regulations 2026, the "No Further Stay" condition, formally known as condition 8503, will become mandatory on all Subclass 600 Visitor visas, Subclass 601 Electronic Travel Authorities (ETA), and Subclass 651 eVisitors for applications lodged on or after November 28, 2026.
Previously, the condition was discretionary on many visitor streams and could not be applied at all to the ETA or eVisitor categories.
Australian High Commission Nairobi announces job vacancies at KSh 244,216 monthly
A person whose visa carries condition 8503 cannot lodge a valid application for most substantive visas while physically in Australia.
Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

The only exception is a protection visa. In nearly all other cases, including those seeking to study, work, or apply for a partner or skilled visa, the applicant will be required to leave Australia and submit their application from outside the country.
Visas granted before November 28, 2026, are not affected, and applications submitted before the cutoff date will be processed under the previous rules.

The Australian government says the aim is to preserve visitor visas for genuine short-stay purposes and to curb what it describes as "visa hopping," where individuals enter as visitors and subsequently apply for successive temporary visas to remain in the country.
The measure forms part of a wider package of migration reforms, including student visa changes introduced in October 2026, all aimed at reducing net overseas migration.
Sweden Offers Foreign Master’s Graduates 9-Month Residence Permit, Eligible Countries Listed
Separately, from November 30, 2026, the Department of Home Affairs will apply a more rigorous, case-by-case assessment to Bridging Visa B applications linked to employer-sponsored visas.
This will cover the Skills in Demand (Subclass 482), Employer Nomination Scheme (Subclass 186), and Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional (Subclass 494) streams.

The legal threshold remains the same, requiring applicants to demonstrate "substantial reasons" for travelling abroad, but the standard will be enforced more strictly, with shorter travel windows tied to stated purposes and specific dates.

General references to holidays or family visits may no longer be sufficient without supporting documentation. The application fee stands at AUD 575, equivalent to approximately KSh 48,000, following a rise from AUD 190 on July 1, 2026.
For Kenyans intending to visit Australia, the central takeaway is that a visitor visa can no longer serve as a first step toward study or employment in the country.
How to apply for a US green card while living in Kenya: Step-by-step guide
Those with plans to work or study should apply for the correct visa before departing Kenya.

For those already in Australia on a Bridging Visa A awaiting an employer-sponsored visa decision, leaving the country without a valid Bridging Visa B will cause the visa to lapse and may bar re-entry.
Waivers of condition 8503 remain available but are granted only where compelling and compassionate circumstances arose after the visa was issued and were beyond the applicant's control.

items.title: Kenya Unveils USD 692 Mn Circular Economy Strategy
items.description: (3 Minutes Read)
content: Kenya has launched the National Circular Economy Strategy and Implementation Plan (CESIP) 2027–2032, aimed at transforming waste into an economic resource, reducing pollution and creating employment opportunities.

Launched on November 24, the five-year strategy seeks to mobilise over USD 692 million in investment by shifting from traditional waste disposal to a circular economy based on reusing, repairing, recycling and recovering materials.

The strategy prioritises five sectors: agriculture and food systems, plastics and packaging, electrical and electronic equipment, textiles and fashion, and mining, quarrying and construction. Environment Cabinet Secretary Deborah Barasa said the initiative would promote resource efficiency, sustainable production and consumption while creating investment opportunities and reducing environmental degradation.

Key measures include strengthening recycling infrastructure, enforcing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), promoting waste segregation at source and encouraging the use of recycled materials through green public procurement.

County governments will work with the national government to improve waste collection, sorting and processing systems. The strategy also seeks to integrate informal waste workers into formal economic structures, improve their working conditions and expand employment opportunities for women and young people.
https://trendsnafrica.com/ethiopian-youth-turn-waste-into-opportunity-33-green-startups-graduate-from-circular-economy-business-incubator/

The government expects the initiative to stimulate local manufacturing, strengthen supply chains, reduce reliance on raw material imports and create opportunities for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Beyond economic benefits, the strategy aims to reduce pollution, minimise waste sent to dumpsites, conserve natural resources and support climate action.
However, its success will depend on effective implementation, sustained financing, strong government coordination and active participation from businesses, investors, consumers and waste workers.

"Light showers": Kenya Met predicts rainfall in some counties over next 24 hours
items.description: Kenya Met forecasts light showers across select counties, thunderstorms along the coast and winds above 25 knots in parts of Marsabit and Turkana in 24 hours.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!
Amos Khaemba is a Current Affairs Editor at TUKO.co.ke, covering general news. Khaemba has over four years of journalism experience and joined TUKO.co.ke in 2022.
Nairobi - The Kenya Meteorological Department has released its daily weather forecast covering all 47 counties, effective from 9.00 pm on November 26, 2026, through to 9.00 pm on November 27, 2026.

Acting Director Edward Muriuki issued the bulletin on November 26, 2026, at 3.00 pm, warning that strong southerly to southeasterly winds exceeding 25 knots (12.5 m/s) are expected over parts of Marsabit and Turkana counties. Rainfall is otherwise expected to remain light and confined to isolated locations across the country.
Kenya Met forecasts rainfall in 39 counties from November 26 to December 3

Along the coast, Mombasa and Kilifi will experience partly cloudy skies tonight before giving way to sunny intervals through the morning. Kwale and Kilifi residents should, however, expect light showers to be possible during the afternoon.

Tana River and Lamu face a more active outlook, with thunderstorms and light showers forecast both tonight and during the afternoon of November 27. Taita Taveta is similarly flagged for light rains and thunderstorms at multiple points during the forecast period.

Further inland, Makueni stands out as one of the counties with the most widespread rainfall activity, with light showers and thunderstorms anticipated tonight, in the morning, and again in the afternoon.

Kitui and Machakos are also in line for scattered showers, particularly in the morning and afternoon hours. Marsabit, specifically around Moyale, is expected to record light showers and thunderstorms overnight.

Nairobi residents can expect partly cloudy skies tonight with a chance of light showers, though no significant rainfall is forecast for the city's morning or afternoon hours. Counties across the Rift Valley, western Kenya , and the Lake Victoria basin, including Turkana, Nakuru, Kakamega, Kisumu, and Narok, are largely forecast to remain dry with sunny intervals through the day.
Kenya Met releases 24-hour weather forecast, warns of rainfall in several counties on November 26

Temperatures will peak highest in Turkana at 37°C and Mandera at 36°C, while cooler conditions prevail in highland areas. Laikipia is set to record a low of 12°C, with Uasin Gishu and Elgeyo Marakwet also dipping to 13°C overnight.
Garissa, Wajir, Siaya, Nyamira, and Kisii are among counties expected to remain largely dry, with partly cloudy skies and sunny intervals dominating through the forecast period.
The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority placed the probability of a strong El Niño developing this year at 81%, with a 97% likelihood that its effects will extend into early 2027.

Rama Afullo: Kenyan Behind a $9 Million Venture Bringing AI Computing to Satellites
items.description: A team of engineers working out of Nairobi and California is helping power a space software startup that has raised more than $9 million (about Ksh1.17 billion) to process satellite data directly in orbit. Founded in…
content: A team of engineers working out of Nairobi and California is helping power a space software startup that has raised more than $9 million (about Ksh1.17 billion) to process satellite data directly in orbit.

Founded in 2024 by 34-year-old Kenyan technology engineer Rama Afullo, San Francisco-based Satlyt builds artificial intelligence (AI) software that lets satellites analyze information in space rather than beaming raw data down to Earth.

Satellites gather critical data for farming, environmental monitoring, disaster response, and security. However, limited onboard computing power forces operators to transmit massive amounts of raw information to ground stations for analysis, a process that is often slow and expensive.
The Mwakilishi Daily News Digest: Kenya and diaspora news, once a day. Free, and you can unsubscribe anytime.

Satlyt’s software solves this bottleneck by running on computing hardware already installed in existing satellites. It allows satellites to process workloads in orbit and communicate as a network, sending back finished insights to operators, companies, and governments.

The system also allows third-party software developers to deploy applications in space without the cost of building or launching their own satellites. For sectors like agriculture, faster orbital processing could help farmers spot crop stress much earlier.
Also read US-Based Kenyan Offers to Raise KSh100 Million for Sifuna’s 2027 Presidential Bid

Before launching Satlyt with backing from venture capitalists, Afullo spent years at major global technology firms. He worked as a Global Product Manager for SpaceX’s Starlink program, where he led efforts to expand global connectivity and customer engagement.

Prior to SpaceX, he spent five years at Google as a Cloud Architect and Solutions Consultant, later managing AI startups. Early in his career, Afullo became one of Tesla’s first three employees in Africa, serving as Telco Business Lead to launch the Powerwall and build energy and telecom partnerships across emerging markets.
Afullo’s path to space technology began at home. His father is an electrical engineering professor who researched microwave and satellite technology, while his mother is a computer scientist.

Raised across Kenya, Botswana, and South Africa, Afullo earned a mechanical engineering degree from the University of Cape Town. He later moved to the United States to complete a Master of Science in Space Systems Engineering at Johns Hopkins University's Whiting School of Engineering.

Today, as Satlyt's chief executive officer, Afullo splits his engineering operations between Nairobi and California, establishing himself as a prominent voice on orbital computing, intersatellite networks, and AI autonomy.

items.description: Nairobi residents with unpaid water bills or illegal connections face heavy financial penalties, reconnection fees, and possible jail terms after the Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company (NCWSC) launched a mass dis…
content: Nairobi residents with unpaid water bills or illegal connections face heavy financial penalties, reconnection fees, and possible jail terms after the Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company (NCWSC) launched a mass disconnection drive on Thursday, November 26.

The operation began in Utawala estate, covering the Mihango area and the wider upper Embakasi region, before expanding to other estates across the city. Under the utility’s enforcement rules, residents caught with irregular connections risk fines of up to Ksh30,000 for domestic use and up to Ksh100,000 for commercial premises, alongside potential prison sentences.

Those whose supply is cut off will also face steep charges to restore services. Water reconnection costs Ksh5,000 plus a double deposit, while sewer reconnection ranges between Ksh15,000 and Ksh25,000 depending on the type of dwelling.

"We are on the ground conducting a mass water disconnection exercise. Pay your water bill early to avoid service disruptions," NCWSC said in a statement.
To prevent wrongful disconnections during the sweep, the company instructed customers with active installment payment plans to place copies of their agreements right next to their water meters.
Also read German Firms Eye New Investments in Kenya as Steinmeier Visits Nairobi
"If you have an instalment payment agreement, display it next to your water meter. Let's pay our water bills so we can enjoy an uninterrupted water supply," the agency added.

The utility said the drive is meant to recover unpaid arrears, enforce payment obligations, and ensure only customers with regularized, legal connections receive water. It urged residents to clear pending bills and formalize their connections immediately.

Thursday's operation extends a series of aggressive enforcement drives in the wider Embakasi area. In May and August 2026, NCWSC carried out similar disconnections in Embakasi East following a grace period, leaving several households without water for weeks.

items.title: Kenya Loses Sh450 Billion Annually to Road Crashes, Chirchir Reveals
items.description: Road crashes are draining about Sh450 billion from Kenya's economy every year, roughly 5 to 8 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product, as highway deaths continue to rise in 2026. Transport Cabinet Secretary Da…
content: Road crashes are draining about Sh450 billion from Kenya's economy every year, roughly 5 to 8 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product, as highway deaths continue to rise in 2026.

Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir disclosed the financial toll on Thursday, November 26, during the opening of the Africa Road Safety Conference 2026 in Nairobi. Official figures presented at the forum show fatalities reached 4,613 by November 16, 2026, up from 4,238 over the same period last year. The upward trend follows a jump in annual deaths from 4,748 in 2024 to 5,009 in 2025.

To reverse the losses, the government is rolling out a Sh30 billion Road Safety Action Plan. The strategy targets a 30 percent reduction in road fatalities by 2028 through legal reforms, automated policing, and infrastructure upgrades.
The Mwakilishi Daily News Digest: Kenya and diaspora news, once a day. Free, and you can unsubscribe anytime.
"The road safety challenge and experience in Kenya reflects the challenges associated with rapid urbanization, population growth and increasing motorization," Chirchir said.

A central pillar of the response is an ongoing review of the Traffic Act, Cap 403. Authorities aim to close existing legal loopholes and tighten accountability to match changing transport patterns and new vehicle technologies.
Also read US to Cut Health Funding to Kenya Gradually Under New Ksh325 Billion Deal

On the roads, the ministry is partnering with the National Police Service to expand technology-driven enforcement. Police are deploying speed cameras, automatic number plate recognition, and digital offense management systems to curb speeding, drunk driving, overloading, reckless driving, and unroadworthy vehicles.
Vehicle inspection centers are also shifting to automated testing and digital records to keep defective vehicles off the road.

For the public transport sector, where operator compliance currently stands at about 76 percent, more than 4,000 drivers and management staff have completed safety training over the past three months. The broader action plan also introduces specific reforms for public transport and motorcycle safety.

To address dangerous road designs, the government is setting up a road assessment program. The initiative will map high-risk corridors, prioritize known accident black spots, and require safety audits during infrastructure planning and funding.

Chirchir urged stronger political leadership, steady financing, and wider use of technology to shield vulnerable road users, including pedestrians, cyclists, and public transport passengers. Globally, road crashes claim roughly 1.2 million lives each year and leave millions more injured.
"Road crashes are not inevitable events. They are preventable tragedies. Every life lost is one too many," he said.

The two-day conference, running from November 26 to 27 at the KCB Leadership Centre, has drawn policymakers, government officials, development partners, and industry leaders. Delegates are examining ways to speed up the African Road Safety Action Plan for 2021–2030, which seeks to cut road deaths and injuries across the continent by at least 50 percent by 2030.

items.title: Green Tech Hackathon Kenya: 267 Applications, 12 Teams
items.description: Oracle and Strathmore ran the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya: 267 applications, 12 finalists, and Team Daraja crowned champion on 16 October.
content: Oracle says student teams in Kenya built climate and sustainability tools on its cloud and low-code stack at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, and the company’s own write-up carries the headline “Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya.” According to Oracle’s blog, the event drew 267 applications, narrowed them to 12 finalist teams, and ended with an in-person pitching day at Strathmore University on 16 October 2026. Team Daraja took the title.

A separate report from @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University, which names Oracle Kenya as a partner, fills in what the winners actually built. It describes Team Daraja’s entry as an AI-powered early-warning tool meant to help farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. That is a concrete, practical product idea, and it is the kind of project a developer audience can judge on its merits.

This story sits on the coding-tools desk because of what the students used and learned. Oracle names Oracle Academy, Oracle APEX and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure as the technology behind the event, and it lists application development, cloud technologies, artificial intelligence and problem-solving as the skills on offer. For readers who track how developers pick up tools, from AI editors (see our Antigravity vs Cursor price comparison ) to low-code platforms, a student hackathon is a useful window into what the next cohort of engineers will reach for first.

The core facts come from two kinds of source. Oracle’s blog post is the main account, and it frames the event as a program for university and TVET students across Kenya. TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students. That matters for the story, because it widens the pool of people who got hands-on time with cloud and application-development tools.

Oracle describes the format as four days of virtual learning, technical mentoring and solution development, followed by the in-person pitching event at Strathmore University. The company identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The @iLabAfrica report, which names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya, confirms the 12 finalist teams and supplies the description of the winning solution.

An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail. It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026. We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran. One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below.

None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student. The reports also give no prize amounts, no judging rubric and no list of the 12 finalist teams beyond the winner. We will not fill those gaps with guesses. Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis.

Oracle reports 267 applications for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. Twelve teams reached the finals, a figure that both Oracle and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report confirm. Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool. We will not turn that into a precise acceptance rate, because the reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individual students or teams. A rate built on an unclear denominator would mislead.
The table below gathers every figure the fact record supports, with the source for each. Treat the right-hand column as the guide to how much weight each number deserves.

The team-size rule is worth a second look. A cap of five and a floor of two pushes students to split work the way a small product team would, with one person on the data model, another on the interface and another on the pitch. That structure rewards collaboration over solo heroics, and it mirrors how real engineering squads operate.

Oracle describes a two-stage design. Students first spent four days online, learning tools, getting technical mentoring and building solutions. The finalists then met in person at Strathmore University to pitch on 16 October 2026. Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection.

The event listing places the virtual bootcamp on 12 to 15 October 2026, which matches Oracle’s four-day count. Four days is short. A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window. Mentoring is what makes this workable, and Oracle lists technical mentoring as a named part of the program.

Low-code tooling helps here. A platform that generates forms, reports and data screens from a database schema lets a student team spend its limited hours on the problem logic instead of boilerplate. Oracle names APEX as part of the toolkit, and we return to why that choice shapes the projects later in this piece.

The 16 October event at Strathmore University is where Oracle says Team Daraja earned the champion title. Pitching in person tests a skill that code alone cannot show, which is the ability to explain a technical solution to non-technical judges. For a climate-focused event, that skill carries extra weight, because the people who fund or adopt these tools are usually farmers’ cooperatives, county offices or NGOs rather than engineers.

The @iLabAfrica report describes Team Daraja’s solution as an AI-powered early-warning tool that helps farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. Oracle’s blog confirms the team as champion but, in the material available to us, the Strathmore account is the one that describes the product. We do not have technical details such as the model type, the data sources, the delivery channel or any accuracy figures, so we cannot say how the system works under the hood.

Even without those details, the problem choice is sensible. Livestock disease, drought and flooding are three hazards that hit smallholder agriculture hard and tend to arrive with some lead-time signal, whether from weather data, soil moisture or reported symptoms in nearby herds. A tool that turns those signals into an early alert fits squarely inside the climate-smart agriculture track that Oracle lists among the event’s challenges.

Here is our analysis, and it is not a reported fact. Early-warning products live or die on delivery. A prediction that reaches a farmer by SMS or a simple dashboard in time to act is worth more than a more accurate model that sits behind a login nobody opens. When Team Daraja or any follow-on partner takes this beyond a prototype, the interface and the alert channel will matter as much as the machine learning.

The win also fits a pattern in applied-AI education. Student projects that tie a model to a real local hazard tend to stand out against generic demos, because judges can picture an actual user. We cannot confirm what the judges prioritized in Nairobi, since no judging criteria appear in the reports. We can say the winning idea matched the sustainability theme directly.

Oracle names six challenge areas for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. They are climate-smart agriculture, waste and the circular economy, carbon reduction, sustainable transport, climate data and water stewardship. The list covers both physical-world problems, such as waste and transport, and data-centric ones, such as climate data. That mix gave teams room to pick a problem that matched their skills.

The reports do not say which tracks drew the most entries, so we cannot rank them by popularity. What we can observe is that nearly every track depends on data collection and reporting, which is exactly what a low-code, database-backed platform handles well. A team building a waste-tracking app or a water-usage dashboard can reach a working demo quickly with that kind of tooling.

Oracle names three technology pillars for the event. Oracle Academy is the company’s education program. Oracle APEX is its low-code application platform. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the cloud where applications run. The table below separates what Oracle reports from general background on each product, so readers can see where the reported record ends.

The last row matters. Oracle lists artificial intelligence as a skill area but does not name the AI services students used, so we do not know whether Team Daraja’s model ran on Oracle’s own AI offerings or on other tools. Readers should not assume the winning system was built entirely inside the Oracle stack.

For infrastructure-minded developers, the cloud piece offers a lesson that carries over from the student setting to professional work. A team that deploys on any major cloud quickly runs into questions of configuration drift, cost and repeatability. Our walkthrough on Terraform drift detection on AWS covers the same habits in a different cloud, and the principles apply whichever provider a hackathon team picks.

Tool vendors invest in student events because first tools tend to stick. A developer who ships a first real project on one platform often carries that familiarity into a first job. That logic explains why Oracle runs Oracle Academy alongside events like this one, and it explains why rivals in the cloud and editor markets run similar programs. The hackathon is a funnel, and the sustainability theme gives it a public-benefit frame.

The tooling mix on display is also instructive. Low-code, cloud hosting and AI skills sit side by side in Oracle’s description, and that matches a wider shift in how software gets built. Many teams now pair a generative coding assistant with a managed platform to cut time to prototype. If you want to see how seat pricing and usage tracking work for those assistants, our GitHub Copilot usage audit shows how engineering leads measure what a team actually uses. For more on this category, browse the software section .

Oracle’s report does not say whether students used AI coding assistants during the four virtual days, and we will not claim they did. It is a fair question for future editions, though. Within a four-day build window, any tool that speeds up scaffolding changes what a team can finish, and organizers will need to decide how to judge work when assistants are allowed.

The record on this story contains two discrepancies, and honest coverage has to name them. First, the event listing gives the in-person pitching date as 16 October 2025, which clashes with the event’s 2026 title and with the reports that state 16 October 2026. We treat the 2025 date as unconfirmed for the 2026 event and use 16 October 2026, the date Oracle and the Strathmore report support.

Second, one official report describes a two-day online hackathon on 14 to 15 October 2026, while Oracle’s account describes four days of virtual work and a program ending on 16 October 2026. Both could be partly right if the online stage had different phases, or one report could simply be describing a different part of the program. The available material does not settle it. The table lays out the conflicts side by side.

None of this changes the headline facts. The 267 applications, the 12 finalists, the Strathmore venue and Team Daraja’s title all hold up across the sources we have. The conflicts affect only the precise calendar, and readers planning to follow the event next year should check the organizers’ own pages for the final schedule.

Hackathons have worked as recruiting and training tools for well over a decade, and technology firms treat them as a low-cost way to meet students. In Kenya, university innovation hubs such as Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica have long hosted this kind of event, and they give companies a ready venue, a pool of students and a mentoring network. Oracle’s choice to partner with a university hub rather than run the event alone follows that established playbook.

Climate-themed hackathons have grown more common as sustainability moved up the corporate agenda. Pairing a green theme with cloud and AI tools lets a vendor show its platform solving problems that governments and donors care about. For students, the theme adds meaning to what could otherwise be a generic coding exercise. We lack figures on how many such events ran in Kenya this year, so we will not size the trend.

Developer culture around tools also shifts fast, and what students learn today may not match what their employers use. Survey data on editor choice shows how slowly some habits change. Our look at Vim, Neovim and Helix usage shares shows long-lived tools holding ground while newer entrants fight for a small slice. Platform vendors know this, which is why they court learners early.

A vendor-sponsored hackathon is one of several ways a student can gain practical skills. The comparison below is qualitative and reflects our editorial view, not measured data. It weighs what each route tends to offer.

The hackathon’s edge is the combination of deadline pressure, a live audience and expert help in one place. Its limit is lock-in, since students leave knowing one vendor’s tools best. A smart organizer balances this by teaching general skills, such as data modeling and cloud basics, that transfer. Oracle lists problem-solving and application development among the targeted skills, which suggests at least some of the learning is portable.

One event will not shift a labor market, and the reports give no hiring or funding outcomes. What 267 applications do show is demand. Hundreds of students wanted four days of cloud and AI training on a sustainability brief, and that is a useful signal for employers, universities and the vendors competing for developer attention.

The TVET angle deserves attention. Open calls that include technical and vocational students bring a different group into the pipeline than events limited to university computer science departments. Employers who need applied builders, rather than researchers, may find that group valuable. This is our reading, and the reports do not break down the applicants by institution type.

For Oracle, the commercial upside is indirect. The company gains goodwill, a base of students who know Oracle Academy, APEX and its cloud, and a story that links its products to climate goals. We have no figures on cost, sponsorship size or conversion to paid usage, so we cannot size the return. The reports contain no prices or product specifications.

Beyond that, local partners gain too. Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica strengthens its position as a convening point for student innovation, and Oracle Kenya gets a visible presence on campus. Winning teams such as Team Daraja may find doors open to mentors, pilots and funders, although no such follow-up has been announced.
These are our forecasts, offered as analysis and not as reported facts. Each rests on the pattern of the reported event.

The most uncertain call is the second one. Judges at one event are a small sample, and a different panel could have preferred a waste or transport project. Treat these predictions as informed expectations rather than certainties.

For students, the main lesson is to anchor a project to a named, local problem. Climate hazards affect real farmers, and a solution aimed at a defined user earns attention in a way abstract demos do not. Keep the team to a small group, split roles early and leave time to rehearse the pitch, since the live stage rewards clear explanation.

For educators, the event shows how a hybrid format can stretch reach. A virtual learning phase brings in students from any region, while a single in-person finale keeps the energy and networking of a live event. Pairing the two keeps costs down without losing the stage.

For engineers building AI features, the Team Daraja idea is a reminder to monitor what models do after launch. A prediction service that drifts or fails quietly can mislead the farmers it aims to help. Our guide to LLM observability in Python walks through tracking cost, latency and tokens, and the same discipline applies to any production AI tool.

Finally, readers following AI coding tools can compare how those products price and perform. The Cursor Composer 2.5 bake-off shows a hands-on method for testing an assistant on a real task, a useful habit for any team, student or professional, that wants evidence before adopting a tool.

Several questions remain open. The reports do not name the judges, the prize, the runners-up or the other 11 finalist projects beyond the winner. They give no technical detail on Team Daraja’s model or data sources. They do not say how many of the 267 applicants were individuals versus teams, and they give no breakdown by university or TVET institution.

We also lack any named speaker or on-record quote. No attributable statement from Oracle staff, Strathmore staff or the students appears in the material, so this article paraphrases the published reports instead of quoting people. If organizers release a results page, a judging summary or a post-event interview, we will update the coverage.

The takeaway: the verified record shows a well-subscribed student event, a clear Oracle technology stack, a sustainability brief and a winner with a practical farming tool. The gaps are real, but the core story holds across Oracle’s blog and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report.

Kenya unveils new renewable energy projects as global delegates convene in Naivasha
items.description: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.
content: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.

The three-day conference, themed Powering Africa in the Green Industrial Revolution, has brought together stakeholders from the energy, finance, government and private sectors to explore investment opportunities and partnerships aimed at accelerating the transition to sustainable energy.

Speaking during the conference, KenGen CEO Engineer Peter Jenga said the company has identified several potential renewable energy projects currently undergoing feasibility studies, which are expected to inject additional megawatts into the national grid.
Jenga said the projects include a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant, an 8.6-megawatt Gogo hydroelectric power project and an 80.3-megawatt geothermal power plant.

“We have already completed the assessment of EPC contractors for a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant. We are also completing the assessment for the Gogo hydro power plant, which will generate 8.6 megawatts,” said Jenga.
He added that the company is exploring small hydro-power opportunities across the country to address challenges associated with reliance on conventional hydro-power generation.
One of the identified sites is in Webuye, where preliminary assessments indicate the potential to generate 26 megawatts of electricity.

The company is also considering wind energy development in Marsabit, which Jenga says has the potential to generate approximately 1,000 megawatts, with an initial 200-megawatt project being considered.
Meanwhile, Canada has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Kenya’s energy transition through investment, technical cooperation and technology transfer.
Canadian High Commission Head of Cooperation Sophie Grace said Canada is keen to explore opportunities in Kenya’s energy sector, including nuclear energy and drilling technologies.
She noted that Canada’s extensive experience in energy production could help Kenya strengthen its capacity and position itself as a regional energy exporter.
“We would really like to help support Kenya to move into becoming a large exporter in the region, and that is one of our goals in this collaboration,” said Grace.

Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) Director of Economic Regulation and Strategy Dr John Mutua called for stronger public-private partnerships to mobilise investments and accelerate the implementation of viable energy projects.
Mutua said collaboration with private investors remains critical in achieving Kenya’s energy transition while ensuring consumer protection and sustainability in the sector.

“As we work towards energy transition and ensuring that Kenya is powered with renewable energy, we hope to match the needs of investors while protecting consumers and ensuring a sustainable energy sector,” he said.

The discussions come as Kenya pursues its ambition of transitioning to a predominantly renewable energy-powered economy by 2034, with strategic partnerships, increased investment and technology transfer expected to play a central role in achieving the target.

The three-day conference is expected to provide a platform for stakeholders to strengthen international cooperation, identify investment opportunities and develop strategies to accelerate Africa’s green industrial revolution.

Kenya drops its FlexPay case, the third fintech reversal since 2022

content: FlexPay, the trading name of Flexitech Group Limited, ran a save-now, buy-later service with Naivas Supermarkets under a seven-year agreement signed in February 2021 and due to run until 2028. Shoppers paid in instalments at Naivas tills, FlexPay kept a 5% commission, and the rest was supposed to reach Naivas within 24 hours.

The arrangement worked for about five years before Naivas said FlexPay stopped remitting collections in early 2026, leaving a shortfall of Sh31.2 million, roughly $240,000. The Directorate of Public Prosecutions recommended theft by agent charges in August.

Detectives arreste d two of the four executives eventually named, Martin Kariuki Maina and Johnson Gituma Mwangi, on 1 September. The other two, chief growth officer Dennis Karanu Mwangi and director Richard Machomba, also faced possible prosecution.
The High Court declined in early October to halt the prosecution , ruling that reputational harm alone does not justify stopping a criminal case already filed.

The case turned anyway. In a letter dated 6 November, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions reversed its own decision , telling the Nairobi Regional Criminal Investigation Officer that a further review of the Directorate of Criminal Investigations’ evidence found the dispute civil in nature.

It directed that the file be closed with no further police action and that Naivas be advised to seek civil redress instead. The partnership that had processed more than Sh3 billion in customer payments over five years was already over by the time that letter went out.

Four days later, High Court judge Roseline Aburili barred police and prosecutors from arresting, detaining or charging the four executives while a separate constitutional petition they had filed, accusing Naivas of using police to recover a commercial debt, is heard.

Public interest is not merely served by securing convictions at all costs, it is primarily anchored on the integrity of the administration of justice. The public must have confidence that the criminal process is even handed.
FlexPay disputed being an agent of Naivas at all, telling the court it was a corporate customer operating a credit account, buying goods on credit and settling the balance periodically.

It counterclaimed that Naivas owed it Sh24 million in unreimbursed customer loyalty points and more than Sh300 million in losses it blamed on price manipulation by Naivas staff, plus a further Sh3.07 million it says it paid Naivas during the dispute but was never credited.
Neither the prosecutors’ decision nor the High Court ruling settled which side’s financial claims are correct. Both remain open questions for whatever court eventually hears the underlying debt.

Kenya’s Asset Recovery Agency filed a money laundering and card fraud suit against the Nigerian fintech Kora and a second firm, Kandon Technologies, in July 2022. The court froze both companies’ accounts for six months while the agency investigated.

By November, the Directorate of Criminal Investigations told the court the allegations were not established and asked that its communication be treated as final. Kora’s chief operating officer said the company had always maintained its innocence.

The Asset Recovery Agency also filed a money laundering case against Flutterwave in 2022, alleging that funds in its Kenyan accounts were proceeds of crime. An initial Sh52.5 million portion of that case was closed in March 2023.

A second, linked case involving $3 million held with co-accused firms Adguru and Hupesi Solutions dragged on until November 2023, when the agency withdrew it after what it called further investigation.

The judge who allowed the withdrawal did not simply grant it. He criticised the agency for filing serious proceedings before finishing its own investigation, calling the conduct inappropriate, negligent, reckless and absurd for an investigative body, and ordered that any resulting liability fall personally on the agency’s director and investigating officer rather than on public funds.
It was inappropriate, negligent, reckless and absurd to an investigative agency.

FlexPay’s case began with a private business partner, Naivas, taking a contractual payment dispute to the police. Kora’s and Flutterwave’s cases began with the state’s own Asset Recovery Agency acting on its own suspicion of money laundering, with no named commercial counterparty driving the complaint.

What connects all three is the outcome. A Kenyan authority with the power to freeze accounts and arrest executives moved first and investigated the underlying claim afterwards, and in each case the claim did not hold up once examined.

Neither the prosecutors nor the High Court has ruled on whether Naivas or FlexPay is actually owed money, so the Sh31.2 million claim, FlexPay’s Sh24 million loyalty point counterclaim and its Sh300 million price manipulation allegation all remain unresolved.

Naivas has not said publicly whether it intends to pursue civil proceedings, as prosecutors advised. It is also not yet clear whether the four executives’ constitutional petition will still proceed now that the underlying investigation file has already been closed.
The first thing to watch is whether Naivas actually files a civil claim, since prosecutors advising that route does not guarantee it happens.

The second is whether three reversed cases in four years change how Kenya’s Asset Recovery Agency and the Directorate of Criminal Investigations screen a complaint against a fintech before freezing accounts or making an arrest, since each case so far has cost the accused company months of frozen funds and public suspicion before the state concluded it had moved too soon.

items.title: Kenya woos foreign investors to partner with Kenya on development projects
items.description: Mudavadi urged foreign investors to bring capital, technology and expertise at Equity Group's investment roadshow today.
content: Kenya is courting international investors to bring capital, technology and expertise to fund development, as the government leans on private businesses to complement stretched public resources.

The push was the main theme of Equity Group’s five-day Trade and Investment Roadshow. The event opened in Nairobi on November 25 and has brought together more than 650 investors, business leaders, policymakers and development partners from 54 countries.
Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said Kenya wants investors who bring more than money.
“Kenya welcomes you, bringing not only capital, but also technology, expertise, market knowledge and confidence in the possibilities of our people,” said Mr Mudavadi.

“Join us as partners in building competitive and sustainable projects that generate attractive returns while creating jobs, expanding opportunities and delivering lasting benefits for our economy and society.”
Equity Group Chief Executive James Mwangi said the private sector’s role in financing development has long been underestimated.

“Businesses are creating thousands of jobs, generating wealth and contributing billions in taxes. The private sector is well positioned to work alongside governments in financing development, driving economic growth and creating opportunities for our people,” said Dr Mwangi.

Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA) Chief Executive Carole Kariuki said local businesses bring established supply chains, entrepreneurial expertise and manufacturing capability to partnerships with foreign investors.

She said such partnerships could help Kenyan firms reach wider markets. She also called for a predictable policy environment to attract investment in sectors such as e-mobility, agro-processing and digital services.
Mary Peschka, the International Finance Corporation’s regional director for Eastern Africa, said investors need mechanisms that reduce risk before they commit capital for the long term.
“Through risk-sharing solutions, sound financial structures and local-currency financing, we can help give investors the confidence to commit capital for the long term,” said Ms Peschka.
She identified regulatory reforms, a pipeline of bankable projects and stronger regional supply chains as key to drawing investment.

The roadshow, which ends on November 29, is connecting investors with government officials and Kenyan companies to identify partnerships in manufacturing, agriculture, financial services and other productive sectors.
The initiative is part of Equity Group’s Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan, which aims to link African businesses with capital, technology, markets and expertise.

items.title: Rama Afullo: Kenyan Behind a $9 Million Venture Bringing AI Computing to Satellites
items.description: A team of engineers working out of Nairobi and California is helping power a space software startup that has raised more than $9 million (about Ksh1.17 billion) to process satellite data directly in orbit. Founded in…
content: A team of engineers working out of Nairobi and California is helping power a space software startup that has raised more than $9 million (about Ksh1.17 billion) to process satellite data directly in orbit.

Founded in 2024 by 34-year-old Kenyan technology engineer Rama Afullo, San Francisco-based Satlyt builds artificial intelligence (AI) software that lets satellites analyze information in space rather than beaming raw data down to Earth.

Satellites gather critical data for farming, environmental monitoring, disaster response, and security. However, limited onboard computing power forces operators to transmit massive amounts of raw information to ground stations for analysis, a process that is often slow and expensive.

Satlyt’s software solves this bottleneck by running on computing hardware already installed in existing satellites. It allows satellites to process workloads in orbit and communicate as a network, sending back finished insights to operators, companies, and governments.

The system also allows third-party software developers to deploy applications in space without the cost of building or launching their own satellites. For sectors like agriculture, faster orbital processing could help farmers spot crop stress much earlier.
Also read US-Based Kenyan Offers to Raise KSh100 Million for Sifuna’s 2027 Presidential Bid

Before launching Satlyt with backing from venture capitalists, Afullo spent years at major global technology firms. He worked as a Global Product Manager for SpaceX’s Starlink program, where he led efforts to expand global connectivity and customer engagement.

Prior to SpaceX, he spent five years at Google as a Cloud Architect and Solutions Consultant, later managing AI startups. Early in his career, Afullo became one of Tesla’s first three employees in Africa, serving as Telco Business Lead to launch the Powerwall and build energy and telecom partnerships across emerging markets.
Afullo’s path to space technology began at home. His father is an electrical engineering professor who researched microwave and satellite technology, while his mother is a computer scientist.

Raised across Kenya, Botswana, and South Africa, Afullo earned a mechanical engineering degree from the University of Cape Town. He later moved to the United States to complete a Master of Science in Space Systems Engineering at Johns Hopkins University's Whiting School of Engineering.

Today, as Satlyt's chief executive officer, Afullo splits his engineering operations between Nairobi and California, establishing himself as a prominent voice on orbital computing, intersatellite networks, and AI autonomy.

items.title: Court clears path for KMPDC to implement oral health practice guidelines
items.description: The High Court has lifted interim orders that barred the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council (KMPDC) from implementing guidelines on the expanded scope of practice for community oral health providers.
content: The High Court has lifted interim orders that barred the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council (KMPDC) from implementing guidelines on the expanded scope of practice for community oral health providers.

In orders issued on Thursday, November 26, 2026, Milimani High Court Judge Patricia Nyaundi lifted conservatory orders granted on August 11, 2026, which had temporarily stopped the Council from implementing the disputed regulatory guidelines.

The ruling followed a hearing in a petition filed by Dr. Kahura Mundia, the Kenya Dental Association (KDA) and another petitioner against the KMPDC, the Cabinet Secretary for Health and other parties.
Justice Nyaundi directed that an application dated November 16, 2026, be heard through written submissions, with the petitioners given 14 days to file their arguments.
The respondents and interested parties were also directed to file their submissions within 14 days of service.
The matter will be mentioned on March 1, 2027, to confirm compliance with the filing directions and issue further directions.
The dispute centres on regulatory guidelines concerning the scope of practice for community oral health providers, which the Kenya Dental Association has opposed.

The association has raised concerns over the proposed expansion of professional roles beyond qualified dental surgeons, arguing that the changes could compromise patient safety and professional standards.
In August, the association obtained interim conservatory orders blocking the KMPDC from implementing the contested decisions pending further proceedings in the case.
With the interim orders now lifted, the parties will proceed with written submissions as the court considers the issues raised in the petition.
